text: More than 1,700 years ago, a man named Mani began to preach a new religion in Mesopotamia.
Mani said he was the last prophet sent by God, after the Buddha, Zoroaster and Jesus.
src: founded by the prophet Mani in Sasanian Mesopotamia around 240 / around 240 he broke with the baptists and began to preach a new religion
Mani presented himself as the last in a line of prophets sent by God, after the Buddha in India, Zoroaster in Persia and Jesus in the West

text: The Persian king Shapur I protected him, and Mani sent teachers to spread his faith east and west.
Later, King Bahram I put Mani in prison, where he died.
src: he gained the favour of the new Sasanian king, Shapur I / Under Shapur’s protection he sent missionaries east and west
under King Bahram I Mani was imprisoned and died in chains

text: Manichaeans believed the world was a mixture of light and darkness, and each soul was a spark of light.
Mani wrote his own holy books, and old copies were found in Egypt, at a place called Medinet Madi.
src: taught that the world is a mixture of light and darkness and that souls, sparks of light, can be freed through knowledge and discipline
Mani, unlike most founders of religions, wrote his own scriptures / In 1930 a hoard of papyrus codices in Coptic was found at Medinet Madi in Egypt

text: Merchants carried the faith along the Silk Road, and the Uyghur ruler Bögü Qaghan took it as his own.
Rulers of many faiths punished its believers, so they often lived in secret.
src: Sogdian merchants carried it along the Silk Road, and in 762 or 763 the ruler of the Uyghur Khaganate, Bögü Qaghan, adopted it
Persecuted by Zoroastrian, Christian, Muslim and Chinese rulers alike / Because the religion was so often persecuted, its communities frequently lived in secrecy

text: In the Turfan oasis, explorers found thousands of pieces of its books, with painted pages.
In southern China, a temple still holds a stone image of Mani carved more than 600 years ago.
src: German expeditions to Turfan in Xinjiang, from 1902, recovered thousands of fragments of Manichaean texts / illuminated pages of exquisite book painting
A temple at Cao’an near Quanzhou in southern China still holds a stone image of Mani as the “Buddha of Light”, carved in 1339

text: The young Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer, a follower, for about nine years before he became a Christian.
Today the word "Manichaean" is used for any view that splits everything into good and evil.
src: Augustine of Hippo, who had been a Hearer for about nine years before becoming a Christian
The word “Manichaean” has survived in European languages to describe any world view that divides everything into absolute good and evil
